children: Jim Vena champions precision in railroading, but played a bit fast and loose with his controversial mega-merger. The Union Pacific
CEO was caught on camera saying he might hike prices "3% to 4% extra" for customers that oppose his company’s acquisition of rival Norfolk Southern
, to “teach you a lesson.” As the $85 billion deal heads into the final stage of a rigorous regulatory review, the flippant remark has the power to derail it.

Union Pacific said Vena’s comment in March was an "offhand" one and that it does not retaliate against shippers. Maybe, but like joking about a bomb on an airplane, authorities will take it seriously. Moreover, by fighting against the video’s release until a Surface Transportation Board judge ordered it earlier this month, the company gifted ammunition to deal opponents at a bad time. It puts the statement front and center just as the US political tide turns and the STB unpicks how competition will be affected by a single operator spanning more than 50,000 miles across 43 states.

The bar is already high. Railway operators are required to persuade trustbusters that a merger enhances competition, not just preserves the status quo. It’s a painstaking process. Union Pacific unveiled its proposal in July 2025 and completion isn’t expected until the second half of 2027.

Although Vena has rallied support, including from trucker Knight-Swift Transportation, boilermakers and legislators, there are shippers, unions and elected officials lined up against his transcontinental railway plan, too. A bipartisan group of senators on Wednesday urged the STB to reject the merger, arguing it would raise prices.
They also called out the deal engineer's “threat.” Rival Canadian Pacific Kansas City

went so far as to use the comment as the basis for asking regulators to torpedo Union Pacific's acquisition plan. Investors have become warier of approval since the video's release, according to Breakingviews calculations.

Although indefensible, Vena’s mouthful of foot is insufficient on its own to warrant scrapping a complicated corporate marriage. The STB, comprising three Republicans and a Democrat with one vacant seat, will scrutinize competing perspectives on prices, jobs, supply chains, cost savings, market share and much more to determine whether Union Pacific will make things better for all stakeholders.

Even with the STB’s blessing, accompanying conditions may be that much more rigorous after factoring in the CEO’s choice of words. Any post-merger oversight also might be especially stringent. More than anything, though, chances are growing that Vena and his shareholders will be the ones who get taught a lesson.
Follow Jeffrey Goldfarb on X and Linkedin.
Public comments on Union Pacific's proposed merger with rival railway operator Norfolk Southern were due on November 18.

An administrative law judge at the Surface Transportation Board, the regulator reviewing the deal, on November 4 ordered Union Pacific to remove a "confidential" designation and make public a video of CEO Jim Vena speaking at a Southwest Association of Rail Shippers, or SWARS, conference on March 17.

"The Board has serious concerns about whether Vena's statement at SWARS — as reflected in the recording — may be influencing certain stakeholders' willingness to participate in this proceeding or share their own views about fear of commercial repercussions," according to the order. "The Board will not tolerate actual or threatened retaliation against a stakeholder for participating in this or any other proceeding before the Board."

In the video, Vena said if the merger doesn't go through, Union Pacific would keep operating. "And if I stick around, which I probably will, I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by 3 or 4 extra percent to teach you a lesson," he said.
Union Pacific said it doesn't retaliate against customers and characterized Vena's remark as an "offhand comment."
